item.title: Surprisingly Adorable Insect Portraits
ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
item.content:encoded:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age.It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed.I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects.From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier.Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware?And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent?I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box.As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle.Type at the prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.The whole harness runs on the PC. is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.From a sentence to a running programOne message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.WarGames, written on the XTClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a under 10 KB.Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in , finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.That call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:And this is what Claude made of it:Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s language.A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. Claude works on the machine through these:Look at the system, list directories, read files as text or hex, find text across files, , , , Create and change files; replaces one piece of a file in placeRun DOS programs and batch files and read back what they printed, up to twelve commands in a call, with a screenshot on requestRead and write memory and I/O portsPC speaker music and coloured CP437 art, , Its own notes, kept in A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in . All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories: On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks first. F3 turns it off. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too.Any model, mid-conversation. lists the providers in and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on. has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads.api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s flowchart LR subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"] direction TB subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"] direction TB UI["Chat screen"] LOOP["Agent loop
Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,
history on disk"] TOOLS["Tools
files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,
memory and ports, speaker"] end NET["mTCP + packet driver"] APP <--> NET end TUNNEL["TLS tunnel
copies bytes"] API["Claude Messages API"] NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API IBM PC XT 5160: 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K, CGA. A PicoMEM card supplies the disk (an image on microSD), WiFi as an NE2000, EMS and a battery clock13,000 lines of C and C++, built with Open Watcom for the 8086 instruction set, 176 KB, the whole harness. , 29 KB, the launcher you typeFreeDOS 1.4 with mTCP for TCP/IPThe Claude Messages API, streamed: tool use, images, prompt caching, message threadsA tunnel on another machine, , or . It copies bytes between a plain port and . It can also hold the API key, so the key never touches the PC’s diskA program ClawDOS runs gets 200K beside the harness, or 450K when the harness steps out31 boot tests in DOSBox-X against a mock API, unit tests that run on DOS, and runs on 86Box’s 8088docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back.You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is .python3 scripts/setup-tools.py # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env python3 scripts/build.py # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk python3 tunnel/tunnel.py # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443 python3 scripts/run86box.py # boot an IBM PC XT At the prompt, type .No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type and send . build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type . Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG).Stop a reply, or clear the inputEffort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max, , , and work from the input box. sends a message from the command line and reopens a chat.Setup in full, real hardware, the image updater, other providers, every settingWhat ClawDOS sends to the API and expects backHARNESS.EXE: the chat screen, the turn, the toolsCLAWDOS.EXE, the launcherThe pieces: screen, console, network and HTTP, the API request writer and stream parser, JSON, history, the tool executors, screenshots and the PNG encoderThe TLS tunnel and the mock Messages APIWhat goes on the disk: the manifest, the system prompt, the tool schemas, the skills, the testsBuild, disk image tools, the emulator runners and test harnessesDOSUNIT.EXE, the unit tests that run on DOSClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its ). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it.

item.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
item.author: Jagmeet Singh
item.content:encoded: A U.S. startup is seeking $162 million in damages and an injunction to impact iPhone and Apple Watch imports to India.

item.title: Backblaze Notice at Collection and Privacy Policy
item.content:encoded:
This section of the Privacy Policy applies if you are in the European Economic Area () or the United Kingdom () and supplements the Privacy Policy.
Under the General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”) and/or the United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation (“UK GDPR”), we are required to have a valid legal basis for processing your personal information, and we must inform you of that legal basis. Our legal basis for collecting and using the personal information described above will depend on the specific personal information concerned and the context in which it is collected. Generally, we will collect personal information from you only when you have consented to such collection, when we need the personal information to perform our obligations under a contract with you (for example, when you create an account or use our services), or where the processing is in our legitimate business interests (for example, to detect and prevent fraud and to analyze usage for analytics, modeling, and business intelligence). In some cases, we may also have a legal obligation to collect personal information from you (for example, to verify your identity when accessing your account or services).
Where we rely on legitimate interests, we balance our interests against your interests, rights, and freedoms and apply appropriate safeguards to protect your personal data.
If we ask you to provide personal information to comply with a legal requirement or to enter into a contract with us, we will make this clear at the time we request that personal information. We will also tell you whether providing that personal information is mandatory or not (as well as the possible consequences if you do not provide your personal information). Similarly, if we collect and use your personal information, we will provide you with our legitimate business interests for such collection and use.
If you have questions about or need further information concerning the legal basis for which we collect and use your personal information, please contact us as provided in the section below. Data Storage, Transfers, and Security We use industry-standard methods of securing electronic databases of personal information. However, you should know that no company can fully eliminate security risks associated with personal information. To help protect yourself, please use a strong password, do not use the same password to access your Backblaze account that you use with other accounts or services, and protect your usernames and passwords to help prevent others from accessing your accounts and services.
Your personal information may be transferred to and processed in the United States and other countries where Backblaze and its service providers operate, which may have data protection laws that differ from those in your jurisdiction.
Where required by law, we implement appropriate safeguards for such transfers, including contractual protections and other legally recognized mechanisms. While your information is outside of your country of residence, it is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction in which it is held and may be subject to disclosure to governments, courts, law enforcement, or regulatory agencies pursuant to applicable law. Your Data Protection and Privacy Rights and Choices If you reside within the EEA or in the U.K., you have the following rights under applicable law, which you can exercise at any time: You can access your personal information that we collect. You can correct, update, or delete your personal information and associated data by logging into your account or contacting us as provided in the “Contact for More Information” section below. You can request deletion of your personal information, subject to certain exceptions. Right to restrict processing: You can ask us to restrict the processing of your personal information where, for example, you contest the accuracy of the data or object to our processing. Right to data portability: Where applicable and technically possible, you can request that we provide your personal information in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format. You can object to the processing of your personal information where we rely on legitimate interests as our legal basis. Right to withdraw consent: Where we have collected and processed your personal information with your consent, you can withdraw your consent at any time. Withdrawing your consent will not affect the lawfulness of any processing we conducted prior to your withdrawal, nor will it affect the processing of your personal information conducted in reliance on lawful processing grounds other than consent. Right to opt out of marketing: You have the right to opt out of marketing communications we send you at any time. You can exercise this right by using the unsubscribe link provided in each email. Please note that even after you opt out, you will still receive service and transactional communications from us. Right to lodge a complaint: You have the right to complain to a data protection authority about our collection and use of your personal information. See the section below for contact details.
We will respond to your request within 30 days of receipt. Where a request is complex, or we have received a large number of requests, we may extend this period by a further two months, as permitted under applicable law. If we extend the response period, we will inform you within 30 days of receiving your request and explain the reason for the delay. We will not charge a fee for responding to your request unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, in which case we may charge a reasonable fee or decline to respond.
If you have an account, you may log in to access, update, or delete your personal information and associated data. If you are unable to access your account, you may contact us using the information provided in the section below. Object or Restrict Data Processing In cases where we rely on your consent to process personal information, you can revoke your consent by contacting us. Revoking your consent does not affect the lawfulness of any processing conducted prior to your withdrawal.
You may manage your cookie and tracking preferences through the cookie and tracking preference center, which may be accessed by clicking the link in the footer of our website or through any other cookie settings mechanism made available on the Platform. Please note that cookie and tracking preferences are generally browser- and device-specific, and data collected before we can identify or authenticate you may not be able to be associated with your account. Profiling and Automated Decision-Making Backblaze does not make decisions about you that produce legal effects or similarly significant effects based solely on automated processing, including profiling. In particular, we do not use automated decision-making to make decisions about your eligibility for services, pricing, or access to functionality. This does not prevent us from using personal information for ordinary business purposes, such as analytics, lead management, marketing segmentation, customer relationship management, fraud prevention, security, or service improvement, where such processing does not produce legal or similarly significant effects concerning you. Data Protection Authorities If you are not satisfied with how we handle your personal information, or with our response to a request you have made, you have the right to lodge a complaint with the relevant data protection authority in your jurisdiction. You may contact the applicable authority by clicking below:
We encourage you to contact us first using the information in the section below, so that we may address your concerns directly. Cookies and Similar Technologies Please read our to learn about our practices regarding cookies and similar technologies.
You may access or modify your cookie and tracking preferences at any time by clicking the link in the footer of our website. The exact choices available to you may depend on your location and the laws that apply to you.
Cookies: Cookies are small data files stored on your device when you visit. Cookies allow us to recognize your device during subsequent visits and personalize your experience based on your preferences. They may also provide information to our service providers to help us improve website functionality and usability.
The Platform may use first-party and third-party cookies, as well as other tracking technologies, for advertising and analytics purposes. First-party cookies are set directly by Backblaze and are used to make the Platform function properly, remember your preferences, and support our internal analytics. Third-party cookies are set by our partners and service providers, such as advertising networks and analytics providers, and may be used to track your activity across different websites to deliver targeted advertising and measure performance.
If you consent to the use of cookies by clicking “Accept All Cookies” when you first visit the website, we will collect certain information from you, including Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, browser types, operating systems, page requests, and average time spent on our website. This data helps us understand website activity, monitor performance, and improve the user experience.
You can set your browser to notify you when cookies are received or to block certain types of cookies. However, disabling cookies may limit your ability to access some features of the website. For additional details on how to opt out of the use of cookies, please review our Cookie Notice.
Analytics: We utilize tools like Google Analytics to collect data about website usage, including pages visited, time spent, search terms, and engagement metrics. This information helps us evaluate and enhance the user experience. For example, to opt out of Google Analytics, you can use the Google Analytics Opt-Out Browser Add-On. For more information about how Google uses your data, please visit “How Google uses data when you use our partners' sites or apps.” Please review our Cookie Notice for information on analytics tools used on the website.
Interest-Based Advertising: We work with third parties, such as advertisers, advertising networks, and data exchanges, to deliver tailored content and advertising based on your online activity. These third parties may use their own tracking technologies, including cookies and pixel tags, to collect information about your interactions with our website and other websites. This data helps deliver personalized advertisements for products or services that may interest you.
To opt out of interest-based advertising through cookies or similar technologies on our website, click the link in the footer of our website and update your preferences in our cookie and tracking preference center. You may also use industry opt-out tools, such as Your Online Choices, where available. Please note that opting out does not mean you will no longer receive ads; instead, advertisements may no longer be tailored to your preferences based on online behavior. Cookie-based opt-outs are generally browser- and device-specific, so you may need to repeat the opt-out process if you use a different browser or device or clear your cookies.

item.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
item.content:encoded: I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says: A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing.In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in .It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.Importantly, Clojure is a very Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating new Perl code on the fly, which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way".Pragmatism and hard-won experienceThe designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful: Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from , hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.Sequences and laziness for powerful in-language data processingApplications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach).Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:All the functions used here are built-ins, including the macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like "this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...", makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally ( is another option for a more statically typed flavor).The right approach to object-orientationHistorically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however. Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of OO-like features.That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability to do true multiple dispatch and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.Built-in support for concurrency and parallelismIt wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many ways, which are interleaved.First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM.Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises, futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the module. It provides two useful things:Channels and Go -like functionality () which makes it easy to work with safe concurrent queues and "share data by communicating".go-blocks with non-blocking primitives that make it possible to write cooperative "green threads" with ease.Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless - Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side programming, among with some unique features like for callback-free concurrency.This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation, Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows, maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great! If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming languages.

item.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: The chief technology officer and co-founder of , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.is co-founder of the security firm . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old , an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ chargedMonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.In July, , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.title: Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid
item.content:encoded: Sir Brian May comments: “The Hera spacecraft acquired these two images on 06 November as it circled the Didymos system at a distance of 29.7 km with a resolution of 2.8 m per pixel, providing the perfect opportunity to create this stereoscopic image. Viewed in depth, the sharpness and smoothness of Didymos’s equatorial ridge is very apparent, compared with the rock-strewn surface of the rest of the asteroid.”Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, adds: “Allowing us to observe in 3D with stereo pairs really makes us feel like we are there – even though these images come from 197 million km away. The result is both spectacular and scientifically meaningful.”

item.title: NINLIVE: The Nine Inch Nails live archive
item.content:encoded: Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. item.title: The Anchor Effect: Why Destination Footfall Doesn't Equal Retail Demand
item.author: Dmitry Poroshin
item.content:encoded: 1. The 50-Million-Visitor MetricOn 30 September 2026, Battersea Power Station's developers announced its 50-millionth visitor since the restored landmark opened in October 2022.The milestone signals destination appeal, not shopfront footfall. It is neither a count of unique customers nor evidence of how visitors move or what they intend to buy.Here, an is a major district destination, not a conventional shopping-centre tenant. Its benefit depends on visitor routes and spending.2. Spatial Divergence in Master-Planned EstatesSource: Wandsworth Council, Table 41; survey: 3 October–7 November 2025.Vacancy ranges from 6% to 38%. Table 41 covers 148 units in completed zones; the report refers to around 150 across the wider development. It records occupancy, not why units were vacant.The datasets cover different periods (the survey was in autumn 2025; the visitor milestone was announced in September 2026) and establish no link between visits and vacancy. Vacancy may also reflect rents, unit size, lease terms or fit-out.3. From Destination Traffic to Storefront ExposureA destination visitor does not necessarily pass every unit, notice its frontage, enter, or buy. The path to purchase has five stages:This is a conceptual measurement chain, not a funnel measured at Battersea. People entering the development. The paths they use. Passages within a shopfront's visible approach area. Passers-by crossing the threshold. Visitors completing a purchase.The stages are not interchangeable: destination visits are not frontage footfall, and frontage footfall is not sales. A side-street shop may receive less traffic than one on the main boulevard, even near the same station. Test this with network analysis and observed counts.4. Proximity, Accessibility, and ExposureThese measures answer different spatial questions:Euclidean buffer - How close is the unit in a straight line?Network isochrone - How easily can pedestrians reach it?Frontage flow and visibility - How many people pass the shopfront? uses a Euclidean buffer, such as a 300-metre circle. It gives a quick overview but ignores railway lines, buildings and inaccessible entrances. uses a network isochrone: the area reachable within a given time along pedestrian paths. A five-minute isochrone measures reachability, not movement; quiet and busy streets may lie within the same area. is pedestrian flow past a frontage and the opportunity to see it. It depends on route choice, entrance position, barriers and sightlines. Network and origin-destination models estimate routes, not actual frontage flow; observed counts or validated mobility data are needed.Two units may both be 150 metres' walk from a station. is visible from the main route to nearby offices; is behind a corner. Their isochrones may match, but A could receive more pass-by exposure. Counts establish the difference.5. Matching Pedestrian Flow to the Occupier's P&LFootfall has no universal commercial value: its importance depends on the tenant's business model, opening hours and customer behavior.A simplified revenue model is:Estimated Revenue = Catchment Footfall × Frontage Capture Rate × Store Entry Rate × Purchase Conversion × Average Transaction ValueThe variables represent catchment volume, frontage capture, entry, purchase conversion and average spend. Use a consistent period; if footfall is counted at the shopfront, omit the first two stages. This estimates sales, not profit.Connecting revenue to occupancy costsOCR = Occupancy Costs/Store Revenue × 100%The Occupancy Cost Ratio compares revenue with rent and defined property charges, such as service charges. Use consistent cost definitions and revenue excluding VAT.High exposure does not guarantee viability. If occupancy costs exceed what achievable revenue can support, the tenant may struggle. OCR is not profitability-gross margin, staffing and other expenses still matter-but it links location quality to the cost of securing it.Different retail formats, different flow profiles Commuters may help, but offices, homes, leisure destinations and repeat customers also drive demand. Lunch and evening patterns may matter more than daily totals; offices, residents and leisure uses contribute at different times.Specialist and appointment-led retail: Showrooms may rely on planned visits and referrals rather than walk-ins; accessibility may matter more than passing footfall.An anchor can generate complementary demand or retain spending in its own restaurants, cafés and shops. The effect depends on tenant category, routes and overlap between offers.6. A Diagnostic Framework for Retail Site Selection.Move from broad context to unit-level evidence:Define the unit and catchment: frontage, entrances, nearby destinations and target customers.Map the pedestrian network: streets, crossings, station exits, restrictions and barriers.Assess routes and visibility: likely origins, destinations and sightlines; validate modelled routes. pedestrian counts or privacy-compliant mobility data across times, weekdays, weekends and seasons. establish whether nearby uses complement or compete with the proposed business. estimate revenue, calculate OCR and compare it with gross margin, rent, service charges, staffing and fit-out costs. Test downside and upside scenarios.A single footfall score cannot capture the commercial case. Identify the assumptions driving the result and the evidence supporting them.7. What Public Data Can and Cannot Tell UsPublic data provides a starting point, not the final answer. show destination activity, not movement between zones, repeat visits, or traffic at a particular unit. Check the counting methodology before treating a milestone as a unique-visitor figure., such as Wandsworth Council's survey, provide occupancy and commercial-use information, not reasons for vacancy, store sales, conversion rates or lease terms. from TfL Open Data and its API portal help establish accessibility. Station-level passenger data does not measure pedestrian movement along individual streets or shopfronts.Combine planning and occupancy records, transport and pedestrian-network data, privacy-compliant mobility data, frontage counts and tenant assumptions.For an individual Battersea unit, these sources cannot show which routes carry the most pedestrians or count shopfront passers-by. That requires geocoded entrances, route analysis and observed or validated flow data. Accessibility maps are not footfall maps.8. Conclusion: Measure the Demand That Reaches the DoorBattersea's visitor milestone and Wandsworth Council's survey describe different aspects of the development: destination activity and vacancy across completed zones. Neither explains an individual unit's performance.Proximity, accessibility and exposure must be kept separate. A unit can be close to an attraction but poorly positioned on pedestrian routes, easy to reach but receive little spontaneous traffic, or busy yet fail to attract customers suited to the tenant's offer.Connect spatial evidence to observed movement and store economics: estimate frontage flow, model sales conversion and test whether revenue supports occupancy costs. That is the difference between measuring destination activity and assessing a retail location.

item.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violationsTo test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.
